summary: This work presents a Josephson junction-based non-Foster impedance matching network designed to achieve broadband signal matching without the bandwidth-sensitivity tradeoff inherent to passive linear circuits, with application to axion dark matter searches. WRSPICE simulations demonstrate power transfer of $-4$ dB across a 40 MHz band (30–70 MHz) comparable to a high-$Q$ resonant capacitive match at a single frequency, with potential bandwidth extension to $\geq 10$ GHz if circuit models remain valid.
motivation: Axion detectors using lumped-element circuits require high-$Q$ resonators for sensitivity, which restricts bandwidth per Bode-Fano limits and implies scan times of tens of thousands of years to cover the full parameter space. Josephson junctions biased to exhibit negative inductance ($L_J = L_{J,0}\cos\phi$ negative for $\pi/2 < \phi < 3\pi/2$) offer an active non-Foster component to overcome these gain-bandwidth constraints.
method: A superconducting loop containing a Josephson junction with critical current $\sim 1$ µA (zero-phase inductance $L_{J,0} \approx 3.3 \times 10^{-10}$ H) is flux-biased to phase $\phi = \pi$ via external bias coil, yielding negative effective inductance that cancels geometric inductance via mutual coupling ($k = 0.3$) over a wide frequency range; power transfer is modeled in WRSPICE using the RSCJ junction model with 0.7 nF per ampere capacitance.
result: The non-Foster circuit achieves $-4$ dB power transfer (versus $-3$ dB for the ideal matched capacitor) across 30–70 MHz with only 13% output power loss from 30 MHz to 70 MHz, compared to narrowband resonant matching; however, stability degrades on millisecond timescales and requires bias current precision better than $10^{-7}$ (100 ppb), mitigable via periodic bias current pulsing every 0.5 µA at 50 MHz drive.
